articles.excerpt: Xianyu (闲鱼), also called Goofish or Idle Fish, is China's largest marketplace for second-hand goods. Cameras, phones, designer clothes, collectibles: a lot of it shows up there first, often cheaper th…
articles.body: Xianyu (闲鱼), also called Goofish or Idle Fish, is China's largest marketplace for second-hand goods. Cameras, phones, designer clothes, collectibles: a lot of it shows up there first, often cheaper than anywhere else. Resellers, buying agents and collectors watch certain sellers closely, because good items go fast. Watching by hand is hard. The site is in Chinese, it is built for the phone app, and a busy shop has hundreds of items that change every day. This guide shows how to turn a Xianyu seller's shop into a table, and how to get a daily list of only what changed: new items, new prices, items that are gone.

articles.title: Google wants to lock Android down, but Droynis teaches you how to stay safe instead
articles.excerpt: Droynis keeps me accountable for the security settings I select.
articles.body: Part of the beauty of Android is its openness. It’s one of the many reasons why I would rather snag a Pixel or Galaxy device ahead of an iPhone. I can choose which default apps to employ, where I get them from, how I set up my phone, and even circumvent some restrictions if I’m feeling particularly spicy. A shortcoming of this borderless design is that Android users can often inadvertently set up an environment with potential security issues. As is so often the case with Android, that particular problem also breeds opportunity, and a new open-source app has jumped in to help Google solve it. It’s called Droynis , and it’s the security auditing tool that should’ve been a part of Android all along.

articles.title: How I Turned a Tiny Wait-State into a Small Revenue Stream

articles.body: The problem I kept ignoring When I built my first AI‑assisted code editor, the biggest complaint from early users was the idle time while the model warmed up. The UI would show a spinner for a few seconds, then the suggestions would appear. Most people just tolerated it, but a handful of power users started asking for a way to skip the wait. I originally thought the solution would be a simple performance tweak, but the underlying latency was baked into the API contract I was using. The only real way to cut the wait was to pay for a higher‑tier endpoint, which would increase my own costs. First attempt: a free workaround My first instinct was to add a free "pre‑warm" button that sent a dummy request in the background.

articles.body: A five-person sales team receives enquiries from several service pages. Some requests require integration expertise, others need a regional representative, and some arrive outside working hours. Forwarding every submission to a shared inbox leaves ownership unclear. A routing workflow should produce a recorded decision and a recoverable next step. Start after durable acceptance Validate the enquiry and save it before promising receipt. Preserve permitted campaign context alongside the enquiry. Use a stable submission reference so later delivery and assignment attempts can be traced. Keep contact matching separate from enquiry creation. An existing contact can submit a new request that needs its own history.

articles.body: Redis 8.12-rc1 folds a side project called redis-roaring into core. It gives bitmaps a second, opt-in internal representation based on Roaring Bitmaps, and a new command, BITRANGEINTARRAY , that reads the set-bit positions straight out of it. The release notes describe this as lowering memory use and speeding up bitmap operations. I wanted to know what that actually means for a bitmap that looks like something I'd really store, not a synthetic all-ones or all-zeros string. There's no official Docker image for 8.12-rc1 yet, so I built it from the tagged source inside a throwaway container (the commands are in "Run it yourself" below).

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission, the first Mars mission in 20 years. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected.
